Overview

Static thermal conductivity values measured in laboratories (often hot‑plate/flux‑meter, steady‑state, dry material) capture only a narrow slice of a hygroscopic material’s thermophysical behavior. For hempcrete and straw bale, the same material can change its k by density, temperature, and especially moisture content over diurnal and seasonal cycles, while simultaneously buffering humidity and storing heat. These coupled hygrothermal effects alter heat flows through walls and their indoor climate impacts in ways a single “k” cannot predict, so static values tend to misrepresent building‑physics performance when used without hygrothermal context. <cite id="8970fd61-0">Several teams investigated the effect of straw type, fiber main orientation, bale density, average temperature, and relative humidity (RH), on the bale's effective thermal conductivity, finding increases with density, RH, and temperature and decreases with higher cellulose content and when fibers are predominantly oriented perpendicular to the heat flow</cite> <cite id="8970fd61-4">Hempcrete has low thermal conductivity and high heat storage, and a two‑year field study showed moisture buffering and an 11‑hour temperature damping, indicating performance beyond static metrics</cite>.

Why static k misrepresents performance

- Static k is steady‑state and dry: Laboratory k is typically derived under controlled, one‑sided heat flux and at low RH, so it misses vapor diffusion, sorption, and two‑way coupling with adjacent layers and airflows that dominate in assemblies. <cite id="8970fd61-1">Hygroscopic materials disperse moisture that enters the material, and many ecological insulation materials behave hygrothermally differently from mineral/plastic insulations; studies under real conditions must also include design flaws like air leakage</cite> <cite id="8970fd61-2">Standards such as PN‑EN ISO 6946 compute thermal resistance from material k, but long‑term monitoring shows moisture varies in straw bale walls and empirical relations link straw moisture to microclimate RH and temperature</cite>.
- Moisture strongly changes conduction pathways: Water vapor condensation/adsorption raises local conductivity and removes air pockets; in straw bales, effective k increases with RH directly because wet material conducts heat more. <cite id="8970fd61-0">High RH relates to higher moisture content in the bale, which badly affects conductivity because of the higher water conductivity</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-2">An increase in water content of 0.08 kg/kg from the dry state raised hempcrete thermal conductivity about 8% at 10 °C and 16% at 40 °C</cite>.
- Density and temperature alter conduction and air paths: Compaction and density increase solid conduction and reduce trapped air; temperature increases molecular collisions, raising k. These effects change the same material’s apparent k by large amounts across in‑service conditions. <cite id="8970fd61-0">Conductivity increases with density and temperature; orientation and cellulose content change air paths and insulation</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-0">Thermal conductivity of hempcrete ranges ~0.06–0.11 W/m·K at 200–400 kg/m3 and 0.12–0.18 W/m·K at 450–800 kg/m3, reflecting density–k correlations</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-1">Thermal conductivity increases linearly with temperature and density; a 67% density increase enhanced k by ~54%, while going from dry to 90% RH boosted k by 15–20%</cite>.
- Hygroscopic sorption and buffering decouple heat and moisture: Hempcrete and straw bale sorb/desorb moisture, exchanging water vapor with the air and buffering RH and temperature. This means heat transfer is modulated by latent processes and by phase changes of bound water, not captured by a constant k. <cite id="8970fd61-0">Straw bales are hygroscopic with moisture buffer values around 1.8 and capillary absorption ~0.0155 kg/(m2·s1/2) due to ~90% porosity</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-3">Hempcrete maintains high moisture diffusion and vapor permeability (~2.3×10−11 kg/(Pa·m·s)), and its specific heat can rise to >2900 J/kg·K at 99% RH; MBV ≈ 2 g/(m2·%RH), surpassing conventional concrete</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-4">Hempcrete exhibits phase‑change characteristics with latent heating, high thermal mass, and low k, offering greater energy savings than cellular concrete due to vapor‑moisture movement that balances indoor RH</cite> <cite id="29d0ccda-0">Hempcrete’s phase‑change characteristics (latent heating, high thermal mass, low conductivity) and vapor‑permeable behavior contribute to energy savings via balanced indoor humidity</cite>.
- Thermal capacity and diffusivity shift dynamic response: Even if static transmittance is high, large specific heat and low thermal diffusivity smooth diurnal swings and reduce peak heat transfer, damping temperatures—effects not reflected in a single k. <cite id="c0830d4e-2">Specific heat capacity of hempcrete is ~1000–1590 J/kg·K; thermal diffusivity drops from 1.48×10−7 to 0.98×10−7 m2/s (dry to saturated), and high capacity can provide better thermal performance than suggested by thermal transmittance</cite> <cite id="8970fd61-4">A two‑year monitoring study in a hempcrete dwelling showed positive moisture buffering and an 11‑hour timeshift of temperatures, evidencing dynamic performance beyond static metrics</cite>.

Material‑specific evidence: hempcrete

- Range and drivers of k: Hempcrete’s k depends strongly on density and mix; increasing binder raises k, and anisotropy (fiber orientation) matters. <cite id="c0830d4e-0">Hempcrete k typically 0.06–0.11 W/m·K (200–400 kg/m3) and 0.12–0.18 W/m·K (450–800 kg/m3), with lower k for higher porous hurd fraction and lower density</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-1">Binder content and compaction influence k; hemp shives’ structure causes up to 30% higher k perpendicular to compaction; k increases with temperature and density</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-3">Binder choice has minimal impact on k, but increased binder fraction increases k; hempcrete’s anisotropy and MBV support hygrothermal regulation</cite>.
- Water content increases k but preserves high vapor permeability: Even modest wetting measurably raises k, yet hempcrete remains vapor‑open, allowing moisture to buffer rather than accumulate; this combination changes effective wall behavior far from static k. <cite id="c0830d4e-2">Adding 0.08 kg/kg water increased hempcrete k by ~8–16% depending on temperature; MBV decreased with higher density, and specific heat was ~1000–1590 J/kg·K; high capacity plus slightly reduced diffusivity in wet states yields better dynamic performance than static transmittance suggests</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-3">Hempcrete’s diffusion coefficient and vapor permeability remain high across low‑to‑mid RH; MBV ≈ 2 g/(m2·%RH) and specific heat up to >2900 J/kg·K at 99% RH</cite>.
- Phase change and latent heat: Hempcrete’s cellular structure behaves like a PCM‑like material, absorbing/release heat during sorption/desorption while maintaining low conductive heat flow—this reduces peaks and swings without thicker insulation. <cite id="29d0ccda-0">Hempcrete exhibits phase‑change characteristics (latent heating, high thermal mass, low k), contributing to energy savings via vapor‑moisture movement that balances indoor RH</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-4">Compared to cellular concrete, hempcrete’s energy savings stem from vapor‑permeable behavior that limits unwelcome humidity fluctuations</cite>.

Material‑specific evidence: straw bale

- Strong RH, density, and orientation dependence: Effective k increases with moisture and compaction; fiber orientation perpendicular to heat flow breaks solid conduction paths, increasing insulation. <cite id="8970fd61-0">Conductivity increases with density, RH, and temperature; orientation perpendicular to heat flow eliminates solid conduction paths, while parallel orientation creates less insulant solid paths</cite>.
- Hygrothermal buffering capacity: Straw bales’ high porosity and capillary action create large MBV and vapor buffering, protecting assemblies from interstitial condensation and altering heat flows via diurnal moisture exchange. <cite id="8970fd61-0">Straw bales have MBV around 1.8 and capillary absorption ~0.0155 kg/(m2·s1/2) due to 90% porosity</cite>.
- Real‑condition variability: Because material variability (straw type, cellulose/lignin ratio, production site) is large, static k cannot capture the spread of in‑service performance. <cite id="8970fd61-0">Research reported wide variability in bale conductivity tied to straw type and production site, reflecting material heterogeneity</cite>.

Assembly‑scale and climate‑scale effects missed by static k

- Hydro‑thermal coupling in assemblies: In walls, hempcrete/straw bale interact with plasters, rainscreens, framing, and air leakage. These details control capillary draw, interstitial moisture, and convective loops, changing effective insulation and thermal mass. <cite id="8970fd61-1">Hygrothermal behavior differs across ecological insulations; air leakage is a major problem in high‑insulation timber frame buildings, leading to moisture problems; studies link air leakage to moisture content changes in cellulose and wood fiber insulations and describe moisture/temperature behavior in wood fiber, cellulose, and mineral wool</cite> <cite id="8970fd61-3">Ventilated rainscreens in straw bale buildings reduce interstitial moisture and mold risk, altering hygrothermal dynamics compared to non‑rainscreen constructions</cite>.
- Field performance vs. lab k: In‑situ tests on hempcrete walls show thermal resistance far exceeding typical static expectations, with additional benefits from air tightness and vapor permeability that reduce energy use. <cite id="29d0ccda-2">Hempcrete’s low thermal diffusivity (1.48×10−7 to 0.98×10−7 m2/s) and high specific heat (1000–1590 J/kg·K) provide better thermal performance than static thermal transmittance suggests</cite> <cite id="29d0ccda-3">A case study using the Heat Flow Meter Method found hempcrete walls offered R≈17, over ten times better than a comparable concrete wall, and highlighted construction aspects (air tightness, thermal mass) beyond pure thermal resistance</cite> <cite id="29d0ccda-4">Measured R‑value for hempcrete walls was ~R‑17, implying substantial energy reduction, while the authors emphasize non‑thermal advantages (carbon sequestration, low embodied carbon, integration with airtight construction) that static k alone cannot capture</cite>.
- Orientation and anisotropy matter in walls: Fiber alignment in hempcrete and bale orientation influence solid conduction paths and thus k in real assemblies, not just in small lab samples. <cite id="c0830d4e-1">Orientation and compaction cause up to 30% conductivity variation; perpendicular fibers break conduction paths, while parallel fibers create less insulant paths</cite> <cite id="8970fd61-0">Fiber orientation and cellulose content reduce or increase effective conductivity, respectively</cite>.

Implications for design and assessment

- Static k underestimates wet‑season insulation needs and overestimates peak heat transfer if used in steady‑state models, because hydration/wetting raises k and reduces vapor permeability; dynamic hygrothermal models are needed. <cite id="8970fd61-0">Higher RH raises conductivity due to water’s higher conductivity</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-2">Even small increases in water content raise hempcrete k by ~8–16%, implying static dry k underestimates in‑service conduction during wet periods</cite>.
- Static k misses moisture buffering and diurnal/seasonal temperature damping, leading to overly pessimistic comfort or overly optimistic energy use predictions; dynamic capacity and MBV should be included. <cite id="8970fd61-4">Two‑year monitoring showed hempcrete buffered moisture and damped temperatures by 11 hours</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-2">High specific heat and modified diffusivity under humidity change the dynamic performance beyond what static transmittance implies</cite>.
- Variability in mixes, density, and construction details means that a single k cannot guarantee performance; hemp‑lime ratios, compaction, and binder type shift k and MBV together. <cite id="c0830d4e-0">Binder-to-hemp ratio and compaction level control k (e.g., 0.06–0.11 W/m·K at low density vs. 0.12–0.18 W/m·K at higher density)</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-1">Binder choice can change k minimally while mix design and compaction have larger effects; hemp‑lime mixes show anisotropy and density effects up to 30% in k</cite> <cite id="8970fd61-0">Variability across straw types and production sites reflects real performance spread</cite>.
- Assembly performance depends on whole‑wall hygrothermal design: rainscreens, vapour barriers, and air sealing change capillary rise and interstitial moisture, altering both buffering and conduction. <cite id="8970fd61-3">Ventilated rainscreens control interstitial moisture and reduce mold risk in straw bale walls</cite> <cite id="8970fd61-1">Air leakage leads to moisture problems and changes material moisture content; hygrothermal behavior of wood fiber and cellulose is strongly affected by assembly details</cite>.

Uncertainties and how to improve assessment

- Hemp‑lime mix variability: Hempcrete’s constituents (hurd vs. shive, binder type/ratio, particle size) change k, MBV, and anisotropy. Standards and labels often report single values; material‑specific characterization and hygrothermal property sets are needed. <cite id="c0830d4e-0">Thermal conductivity depends on binder-to-hemp ratio and compaction; higher porous hurd reduces k and density</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-1">Orientation and compaction drive substantial k variation; binder choice can matter less than mix design</cite>.
- Limited controlled field data: While case studies show improved R‑values and dynamic performance, more replicated field measurements and dynamic models integrating sorption, diffusion, and phase change are needed to quantify generalizable deltas. <cite id="29d0ccda-3">Case study provides in‑situ R‑value and practical instrumentation insights, calling for more comprehensive life‑cycle and field data</cite>.
- Practical guidance: Use hygrothermal modeling with moisture‑dependent k and capacity/diffusivity, include MBV and vapor diffusion coefficients, and calibrate with in‑situ measurements when possible. For hygroscopic insulations like hempcrete/straw bale, static dry k should be a lower bound for conduction in wet states and an incomplete proxy for comfort and durability. <cite id="c0830d4e-2">Thermal diffusivity and specific heat vary with humidity; high capacity and permeability in hempcrete can yield better dynamic thermal performance than static transmittance suggests</cite> <cite id="8970fd61-0">Effective conductivity depends on RH, density, and orientation, all of which vary in real walls</cite>.

Bottom line

Static k values are one‑dimensional snapshots that ignore moisture sorption, vapor diffusion, phase change, and assembly‑level hygrothermal coupling. In hygroscopic insulations like hempcrete and straw bale, water uptake raises conductive heat transfer but the same materials also increase thermal capacity, buffer humidity and damp temperature swings, and maintain vapor permeability, all of which reduce peak heat loads and improve comfort beyond what static numbers predict. Consequently, using only static k in building‑physics design tends to underestimate wet‑season heat transfer and overestimate the “penalty” of hygroscopic insulation, while failing to capture its buffering and thermal‑mass benefits; hygrothermal characterization and dynamic modeling are required to reflect true in‑service performance. <cite id="8970fd61-0">Effective thermal conductivity in straw bales increases with RH, density, and temperature, while hygroscopic buffering (MBV ~1.8) disperses moisture</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-2">In hempcrete, modest wetting increases k by ~8–16% but high specific heat and permeability improve dynamic performance beyond static transmittance</cite> <cite id="8970fd61-4">Field monitoring of hempcrete walls demonstrated strong moisture buffering and significant temperature damping, indicating performance that static k cannot represent</cite> <cite id="29d0ccda-2">Hempcrete’s low diffusivity and high capacity provide better thermal performance than static k implies</cite> <cite id="29d0ccda-4">Measured hempcrete wall R‑values exceeded concrete walls, with additional advantages in air tightness, carbon sequestration, and thermal mass</cite>.

Title: Hygrothermal Performance of Bio-Based Exterior Wall Constructions and Their Resilience under Air Leakage and Moisture Load
Snippet: For multi-storey buildings, the combination of external timber frame walls and internal massive timber walls is a particularly ecological construction method [9]. Timber framing, particularly for external walls, offers the opportunity to achieve high insulation thicknesses and thus reduce the operational environmental impact through reduced heating requirements during the cold seasons. However, the most commonly used mineral or plastic-based building materials for thermal insulation are currently responsible for approximately 26.1% of the total embodied CO 2 in construction [10]. Recent research shows that timber constructions with insulation that has a hygrothermal behaviour similar to that of wood are generally more robust and, therefore, more durable [11]. There is a broad consensus that hygroscopic materials disperse moisture that enters the material and thus protect the timber structure. However, there are many different ecological insulation materials, all of which behave hygrothermally differently. Natural fibre insulation materials are based on a wide range of bio-based raw materials, such as wood, cellulose, hemp, jute, and straw [11]. Among the many different types of insulation, wood fibre-based building materials have been extensively investigated hygrothermally [12][13][14]. While straw bale insulation has been known for a relatively long time as an eco-insulation, blowing in chopped straw insulation is a new technology that has recently been increasingly investigated [15]. Previous studies have focused on the risk of mould [16], specific material mixtures such as chopped straw and cellulose [17], or thermal conductivity [15,18]. The hygrothermal properties of sheep's wool [19] and cellulose [20] have also been extensively studied under laboratory conditions. Investigations under real conditions should also include design flaws that may lead to air leakage. Air leakage is generally a major problem in highly insulated timber frame buildings, often leading to moisture problems such as mould [21,22]. Various studies have focused on the relation of air leakage and moisture content of different insulation materials such as cellulose [23,24] and wood fibre [13], and the moisture and temperature behaviour of wood fibre, cellulose, and mineral wool [25].

Title: Mechanical, Thermal, and Moisture Buffering Properties of Novel Insulating Hemp-Lime Composite Building Materials
Snippet: Hempcrete, made of the hemp plant's inner woody core mixed with a lime-based binder, is a promising lightweight biocomposite material that holds the potential to considerably improve energy and indoor environmental performance and sustainability of buildings [1,2]. Nevertheless, the utilization of hempcrete in the construction industry remains low, mainly due to the high variability of hemp-lime composites and lack of formulas that use widely available and locally sourced ingredients. For example, hempcrete's production cost and embodied energy could be considerably higher in Canada than in Europe due to imported materials [3]. The use of innovative binders and a better understanding of the material's performance are indispensable steps for addressing hempcrete underutilization. 

Previous studies have shown that hempcrete hygrothermal and mechanical properties depended on various factors. The binder to hemp ratio, compaction level, water content, and binder mix design have been considered to be critical [4][5][6][7]. For instance, an increase in the proportion of porous hemp hurd in hempcrete mixture reduced the dry density and the thermal conductivity [6,8]. In contrast, there was a positive correlation between density and thermal conductivity of the hempcrete [9,10]. Thus, studies have reported thermal conductivity in the range of 0.06−0.11 W/m K for hempcrete mixtures with dry densities ranging from 200 to 400 kg/m 3 and hemp/binder ratios of 1:1, 1:1.5, and 1:2 [11,12]. In comparison, hempcrete samples with higher dry density and hemp/binder ratio in the range of 450−800 kg/m 3 and 1:2−1:4, respectively, had higher thermal conductivity ranging from 0.12 to 0.18 W/m K [11,12]. Previous findings have also indicated a negative correlation between hempcrete's density and moisture buffering capacity.

Overview

Static thermal conductivity values measured in laboratories (often hot‑plate/flux‑meter, steady‑state, dry material) capture only a narrow slice of a hygroscopic material’s thermophysical behavior. For hempcrete and straw bale, the same material can change its k by density, temperature, and especially moisture content over diurnal and seasonal cycles, while simultaneously buffering humidity and storing heat. These coupled hygrothermal effects alter heat flows through walls and their indoor climate impacts in ways a single “k” cannot predict, so static values tend to misrepresent building‑physics performance when used without hygrothermal context. <cite id="8970fd61-0">Several teams investigated the effect of straw type, fiber main orientation, bale density, average temperature, and relative humidity (RH), on the bale's effective thermal conductivity, finding increases with density, RH, and temperature and decreases with higher cellulose content and when fibers are predominantly oriented perpendicular to the heat flow</cite> <cite id="8970fd61-4">Hempcrete has low thermal conductivity and high heat storage, and a two‑year field study showed moisture buffering and an 11‑hour temperature damping, indicating performance beyond static metrics</cite>.

- Static k is steady‑state and dry: Laboratory k is typically derived under controlled, one‑sided heat flux and at low RH, so it misses vapor diffusion, sorption, and two‑way coupling with adjacent layers and airflows that dominate in assemblies. <cite id="8970fd61-1">Hygroscopic materials disperse moisture that enters the material, and many ecological insulation materials behave hygrothermally differently from mineral/plastic insulations; studies under real conditions must also include design flaws like air leakage</cite> <cite id="8970fd61-2">Standards such as PN‑EN ISO 6946 compute thermal resistance from material k, but long‑term monitoring shows moisture varies in straw bale walls and empirical relations link straw moisture to microclimate RH and temperature</cite>.
- Moisture strongly changes conduction pathways: Water vapor condensation/adsorption raises local conductivity and removes air pockets; in straw bales, effective k increases with RH directly because wet material conducts heat more. <cite id="8970fd61-0">High RH relates to higher moisture content in the bale, which badly affects conductivity because of the higher water conductivity</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-2">An increase in water content of 0.08 kg/kg from the dry state raised hempcrete thermal conductivity about 8% at 10 °C and 16% at 40 °C</cite>.
- Density and temperature alter conduction and air paths: Compaction and density increase solid conduction and reduce trapped air; temperature increases molecular collisions, raising k. These effects change the same material’s apparent k by large amounts across in‑service conditions. <cite id="8970fd61-0">Conductivity increases with density and temperature; orientation and cellulose content change air paths and insulation</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-0">Thermal conductivity of hempcrete ranges ~0.06–0.11 W/m·K at 200–400 kg/m3 and 0.12–0.18 W/m·K at 450–800 kg/m3, reflecting density–k correlations</cite> <cite id="c0830d4e-1">Thermal conductivity increases linearly with temperature and density; a 67% density increase enhanced k by ~54%, while going from dry to 90% RH boosted k by 15–20%</cite>.

Material‑specific evidence: hempcrete

[15] found that the density of barley straw bales ranges from 54.6 kg/m 3 to 78.3 kg/m 3 , whereas that of oat and wheat straw bales ranges from 81 kg/m 3 to 106.3 kg/m 3 . Straw bales are classified as hygroscopic materials with moisture buffer values around 1.8 and capillary absorption of about 0.0155 kg/(m 2 .s 1 /2 ), due to their 90% porosity [16]. Several teams investigated the effect of straw type, fiber main orientation, bale density, average temperature, and relative humidity (RH), on the bale's effective thermal conductivity. The methodology was mainly experimental, using the hot guarded plate technique or flux meters to measure the thermal conductivity. It was found that the latter increases with increasing density, RH, and temperature, and decreases with higher cellulose content and when the fibers are predominantly oriented perpendicular to the heat flow. Increasing density reduces the amount of air trapped inside the bale, which explains the adverse effect on conductivity. High RH relates to the higher moisture content in the bale, which badly affects the conductivity because of the higher water conductivity. When the bale temperature rises, the number of molecules colliding increases due to the higher microscopic kinetic energy, thus increasing the thermal conductivity. Straw type relates to cellulose content and a reduced amount of lignin increases the thermally insulating porous microstructure. Last, when fibers are perpendicular to the heat flow, there is no solid conduction path through the bale, whereas in the parallel case, such paths are through the fibers, which are less insulant than air.

Title: Hygrothermal Performance of Bio-Based Exterior Wall Constructions and Their Resilience under Air Leakage and Moisture Load
Snippet: For multi-storey buildings, the combination of external timber frame walls and internal massive timber walls is a particularly ecological construction method [9]. Timber framing, particularly for external walls, offers the opportunity to achieve high insulation thicknesses and thus reduce the operational environmental impact through reduced heating requirements during the cold seasons. However, the most commonly used mineral or plastic-based building materials for thermal insulation are currently responsible for approximately 26.1% of the total embodied CO 2 in construction [10]. Recent research shows that timber constructions with insulation that has a hygrothermal behaviour similar to that of wood are generally more robust and, therefore, more durable [11]. There is a broad consensus that hygroscopic materials disperse moisture that enters the material and thus protect the timber structure. However, there are many different ecological insulation materials, all of which behave hygrothermally differently. Natural fibre insulation materials are based on a wide range of bio-based raw materials, such as wood, cellulose, hemp, jute, and straw [11]. Among the many different types of insulation, wood fibre-based building materials have been extensively investigated hygrothermally [12][13][14]. While straw bale insulation has been known for a relatively long time as an eco-insulation, blowing in chopped straw insulation is a new technology that has recently been increasingly investigated [15]. Previous studies have focused on the risk of mould [16], specific material mixtures such as chopped straw and cellulose [17], or thermal conductivity [15,18]. The hygrothermal properties of sheep's wool [19] and cellulose [20] have also been extensively studied under laboratory conditions. Investigations under real conditions should also include design flaws that may lead to air leakage. Air leakage is generally a major problem in highly insulated timber frame buildings, often leading to moisture problems such as mould [21,22]. Various studies have focused on the relation of air leakage and moisture content of different insulation materials such as cellulose [23,24] and wood fibre [13], and the moisture and temperature behaviour of wood fibre, cellulose, and mineral wool [25].

Title: The Influence of Ventilated Rainscreens on the Interstitial Hygrothermal Environment of Straw Bale Walls
Snippet: Previous research has found that rainscreens help control interstitial moisture in straw bale walls (Carfrae et al., 2009;Lawrence et al., 2009;Otto et al., 2008;Thompson, 2006). 

The indoor, outdoor and interstitial hygrothermal environment of six straw bale structures in Japan have been monitored. These six straw bale buildings are organized into two groups according to construction details (Fig. 1., Table 1.). The first Group A includes buildings consisting of straw bale walls with an earthen or lime plastered exterior finish applied directly to the bale walls. The second Group B includes buildings consisting of straw bale walls utilizing ventilated rain screens. 

The purpose of the present study is to (one) evaluate the potential for mold growth in the six buildings, (two) clarify moisture dynamics, and (three) determine the effectiveness of ventilated rainscreens to control moisture in straw bale walls.

Title: Mechanical, Thermal, and Moisture Buffering Properties of Novel Insulating Hemp-Lime Composite Building Materials
Snippet: Hempcrete, made of the hemp plant's inner woody core mixed with a lime-based binder, is a promising lightweight biocomposite material that holds the potential to considerably improve energy and indoor environmental performance and sustainability of buildings [1,2]. Nevertheless, the utilization of hempcrete in the construction industry remains low, mainly due to the high variability of hemp-lime composites and lack of formulas that use widely available and locally sourced ingredients. For example, hempcrete's production cost and embodied energy could be considerably higher in Canada than in Europe due to imported materials [3]. The use of innovative binders and a better understanding of the material's performance are indispensable steps for addressing hempcrete underutilization. 

Previous studies have shown that hempcrete hygrothermal and mechanical properties depended on various factors. The binder to hemp ratio, compaction level, water content, and binder mix design have been considered to be critical [4][5][6][7]. For instance, an increase in the proportion of porous hemp hurd in hempcrete mixture reduced the dry density and the thermal conductivity [6,8]. In contrast, there was a positive correlation between density and thermal conductivity of the hempcrete [9,10]. Thus, studies have reported thermal conductivity in the range of 0.06−0.11 W/m K for hempcrete mixtures with dry densities ranging from 200 to 400 kg/m 3 and hemp/binder ratios of 1:1, 1:1.5, and 1:2 [11,12]. In comparison, hempcrete samples with higher dry density and hemp/binder ratio in the range of 450−800 kg/m 3 and 1:2−1:4, respectively, had higher thermal conductivity ranging from 0.12 to 0.18 W/m K [11,12]. Previous findings have also indicated a negative correlation between hempcrete's density and moisture buffering capacity.

Title: State of the Art Review of Attributes and Mechanical Properties of Hempcrete
Snippet: Hemp shives' variable composition and structure affect hempcrete's thermal conductivity, which can increase by up to 30% when heat flows perpendicular to compaction. Its heat conductivity can be influenced by factors like orientation, compaction, and application method, impacting mechanical properties as well. While binder choice does not significantly affect thermal properties, it can impact mechanical performance. Increased wetness, temperature, and density can enhance thermal conductivity and mechanical characteristics, respectively. Recent research suggests that silica sol binder in hempcrete allows for maintained mechanical strength with thermal conductivity similar to hemp shives. Interestingly, smaller hemp shiv particles enhance mechanical strength without affecting thermal conductivity. Yet, in contrast, smaller particles in hemp plaster reduce thermal conductivity, necessitating further study [64,77,78,[114][115][116][117][118][119][120][121][122]. snippet.text: Given that over 95% of buildings are residential, there is an urgent need for carbon-storing materials and easy-to-construct methods to achieve energy-efficient and low-carbon homes, which can significantly impact CO2 reduction. Industrial hemp, used to produce hempcrete, is a promising construction material. Hempcrete, composed of hemp hurd and fibers mixed with lime and water, is currently used for thermal insulation and lightweight building blocks, intended for use in constructing non-load-bearing walls. With growing interest in hempcrete for home construction and a lack of comprehensive data on its performance, a case study assessed the thermal resistance of walls in a home retrofitted with hempcrete insulation in wood-framed walls. This paper focuses on practical in-situ instrumentation and determination of the thermal resistance of hempcrete walls in a retrofitted house. It also provides some basic background information on hemp and hempcrete. It discusses the practical application of the Heat Flow Meter Method for in-situ measurement of the thermal properties of hempcrete walls. The paper concludes with the developed thermal resistance of retrofitted hempcrete walls based on in-situ testing.

Summary

Hempcrete’s hygroscopic “moisture buffering” means its porous hemp hurd aggregate and lime binder adsorb and desorb water in response to ambient humidity, stabilizing wall RH and reducing the need for mechanical heating/cooling. This buffering arises from the high hygroscopic surface area and capillarity of hemp hurds and the chemically sorbing properties of lime, but it imposes material-process trade‑offs that increase embodied carbon relative to dense, low‑porosity conventional concrete. Mechanistically, buffering requires more absorbent and sorbent material (hemp hurds) and often higher lime dosages to fill capillary networks and ensure workability/set, while also increasing demands for protection against moisture-driven degradation; lime itself is energy‑intensive and only partially sequesters CO2 via carbonation, leaving a higher upstream footprint than conventional cement‑concrete assemblies. Despite this, hempcrete’s buffering can reduce operational energy and enable negative cradle‑to‑gate carbon over time in favorable conditions, so the net life‑cycle outcome depends on material choices, thickness/density, transport, and climate.

How hygroscopic buffering raises embodied carbon in hempcrete

1) Material composition and porosity drive greater absorbent mass and binder use  
Hemp hurds are highly porous and hygroscopic, absorbing large amounts of water with little volume change, which gives hempcrete strong moisture buffer capacity but also increases the amount of sorbent aggregate and open porosity in the matrix. <cite id="ad8be665-0">Hemp tree stems have a highly porous anatomy enabling absorption of large water amounts with little volume change, and hemp-based concrete products are used to control moisture in buildings</cite>. <cite id="2472abbd-0">Hemp concrete exhibits a moisture buffer value (MBV) of about 2 g/(m2·%RH), far above traditional concrete’s ~0.37 g/(m2·%RH), reflecting its strong ability to adsorb/release moisture</cite>. <cite id="2472abbd-4">Hemp hurds can absorb up to ~56% bound moisture and rapidly equilibrate via diffusion and vapor permeability; their adsorption rate (0.57–0.66) exceeds desorption (0.27–0.35) at 80–90% RH, implying hygroscopic hysteresis that increases buffering mass and slows release</cite>. <cite id="2472abbd-0">Under daily RH cycling between 33% and 80% at 405–510 kg/m3 densities, hemp concrete showed mass gains >110 g/m2 and steaming depth >4 cm</cite>. 

Because hempcrete’s voids are largely unfilled with hemp hurds rather than compact cement paste, designers often increase binder dosage to achieve comparable workability and early set, raising embodied carbon. <cite id="ad8be665-2">Unlike conventional concrete, hempcrete’s shiv voids are not necessarily filled with lime binder, enhancing insulation; but lime’s high pH confers antimicrobial protection and the high moisture storage capacity arises from hemp’s hygroscopicity</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-2">To reach similar consistency, hempcrete plasters require greater binder than sand–lime coatings, leading to a more substantial carbon footprint</cite>. In practice, this means the hygroscopic “service” of buffering is paid for in material inputs (more lime and hemp hurds), which directly elevates upstream energy, water, and emissions.

2) Lime’s energy intensity and carbonation dynamics  
Hempcrete relies on lime as a binder; while lime can capture CO2 during and after hardening, its upstream energy intensity and slower, incomplete carbonation relative to cement create a higher cradle‑to‑gate footprint. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-0">Hemp shives are a waste product but lime is energy‑intensive; substituting lime with unfired binders reduced total building energy and carbon to ~50–10% of a conventional building over 50 years</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-2">Calcitic lime can capture ~90% of CO2 per kg of lime, but carbonation reabsorption can be less complete than in mineral aggregate mortars due to setting challenges in plant-based concretes; many hempcrete LCAs did not fully account for this</cite>. <cite id="ad8be665-4">The carbon footprint of hempcrete depends on binder type, dosage, transport, and application; plant-based products can have favorable overall life-cycle balance yet higher upfront cost</cite>. 

The buffering function is enabled by lime’s sorption of water and CO2; buffering capacity is enhanced by higher lime surface area and porosity, which again increases binder mass and energy. In unfavorable conditions (high RH, freeze–thaw), lime protection layers and coatings may be required, further adding embodied carbon. <cite id="ad8be665-2">Lime’s alkaline surface protects hemp from mold under humidity/temperature swings that harm other insulations; hempcrete’s high moisture storage and breathability suit diverse climates</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Untreated hempcrete can sequester −15.27 to −8.92 kg CO2e/m2, but sol–gel coated hempcrete showed 22.51–28.77 kg CO2e/m2, still far below 122.71 kg CO2e/m2 for traditional cavity walls</cite>. Snippet: Hemp concrete or "hempcrete" is made of lime, water, and hemp shives, a by-product of fiber processing from hemp stalk. It is a bio-composite material used as an alternative to concrete for construction and insulation. Hempcrete is "carbon-negative" or "better-thanzero-carbon" because hemp plant absorbs more carbon from the air during growth than it yields during its production. Moreover, it continues to absorb carbon after being employed in construction, storing more carbon over the building's lifetime than was emitted during construction [42]. In 2021, Pierre Chevet Sports Centre was built in France as the first public building using hemp concrete as the main construction material [43]. Moreover, preliminary 3D-printing research shows that hempcrete is printable with a density as low as 660 kg/m 3 , with adequate buildability and compressive strength for printing individual walls [44]. Such technical progress will widen the uses of hemp and the possibility to alleviate the negative impact of the construction industry on the environment.

Summary

Hempcrete’s hygroscopic “moisture buffering” means its porous hemp hurd aggregate and lime binder adsorb and desorb water in response to ambient humidity, stabilizing wall RH and reducing the need for mechanical heating/cooling. This buffering arises from the high hygroscopic surface area and capillarity of hemp hurds and the chemically sorbing properties of lime, but it imposes material-process trade‑offs that increase embodied carbon relative to dense, low‑porosity conventional concrete. Mechanistically, buffering requires more absorbent and sorbent material (hemp hurds) and often higher lime dosages to fill capillary networks and ensure workability/set, while also increasing demands for protection against moisture-driven degradation; lime itself is energy‑intensive and only partially sequesters CO2 via carbonation, leaving a higher upstream footprint than conventional cement‑concrete assemblies. Despite this, hempcrete’s buffering can reduce operational energy and enable negative cradle‑to‑gate carbon over time in favorable conditions, so the net life‑cycle outcome depends on material choices, thickness/density, transport, and climate.

How hygroscopic buffering raises embodied carbon in hempcrete

1) Material composition and porosity drive greater absorbent mass and binder use  
Hemp hurds are highly porous and hygroscopic, absorbing large amounts of water with little volume change, which gives hempcrete strong moisture buffer capacity but also increases the amount of sorbent aggregate and open porosity in the matrix. <cite id="ad8be665-0">Hemp tree stems have a highly porous anatomy enabling absorption of large water amounts with little volume change, and hemp-based concrete products are used to control moisture in buildings</cite>. <cite id="2472abbd-0">Hemp concrete exhibits a moisture buffer value (MBV) of about 2 g/(m2·%RH), far above traditional concrete’s ~0.37 g/(m2·%RH), reflecting its strong ability to adsorb/release moisture</cite>. <cite id="2472abbd-4">Hemp hurds can absorb up to ~56% bound moisture and rapidly equilibrate via diffusion and vapor permeability; their adsorption rate (0.57–0.66) exceeds desorption (0.27–0.35) at 80–90% RH, implying hygroscopic hysteresis that increases buffering mass and slows release</cite>. <cite id="2472abbd-0">Under daily RH cycling between 33% and 80% at 405–510 kg/m3 densities, hemp concrete showed mass gains >110 g/m2 and steaming depth >4 cm</cite>. 

Because hempcrete’s voids are largely unfilled with hemp hurds rather than compact cement paste, designers often increase binder dosage to achieve comparable workability and early set, raising embodied carbon. <cite id="ad8be665-2">Unlike conventional concrete, hempcrete’s shiv voids are not necessarily filled with lime binder, enhancing insulation; but lime’s high pH confers antimicrobial protection and the high moisture storage capacity arises from hemp’s hygroscopicity</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-2">To reach similar consistency, hempcrete plasters require greater binder than sand–lime coatings, leading to a more substantial carbon footprint</cite>. In practice, this means the hygroscopic “service” of buffering is paid for in material inputs (more lime and hemp hurds), which directly elevates upstream energy, water, and emissions.

2) Lime’s energy intensity and carbonation dynamics  
Hempcrete relies on lime as a binder; while lime can capture CO2 during and after hardening, its upstream energy intensity and slower, incomplete carbonation relative to cement create a higher cradle‑to‑gate footprint. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-0">Hemp shives are a waste product but lime is energy‑intensive; substituting lime with unfired binders reduced total building energy and carbon to ~50–10% of a conventional building over 50 years</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-2">Calcitic lime can capture ~90% of CO2 per kg of lime, but carbonation reabsorption can be less complete than in mineral aggregate mortars due to setting challenges in plant-based concretes; many hempcrete LCAs did not fully account for this</cite>. <cite id="ad8be665-4">The carbon footprint of hempcrete depends on binder type, dosage, transport, and application; plant-based products can have favorable overall life-cycle balance yet higher upfront cost</cite>. 

The buffering function is enabled by lime’s sorption of water and CO2; buffering capacity is enhanced by higher lime surface area and porosity, which again increases binder mass and energy. In unfavorable conditions (high RH, freeze–thaw), lime protection layers and coatings may be required, further adding embodied carbon. <cite id="ad8be665-2">Lime’s alkaline surface protects hemp from mold under humidity/temperature swings that harm other insulations; hempcrete’s high moisture storage and breathability suit diverse climates</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Untreated hempcrete can sequester −15.27 to −8.92 kg CO2e/m2, but sol–gel coated hempcrete showed 22.51–28.77 kg CO2e/m2, still far below 122.71 kg CO2e/m2 for traditional cavity walls</cite>. The coating example shows how moisture management enhancements can increase embodied emissions; the same logic applies to thicker layers or protective sealants to maintain performance in wet climates.

3) Internal curing and early-age strength demands  
Hemp’s hygroscopicity can be leveraged to internally cure dense concretes by supplying water during hydration, which can reduce autogenous shrinkage and aid early strength; this typically requires higher binder contents or more aggressive curing regimes, again increasing embodied carbon. <cite id="ad8be665-0">Hemp’s hygroscopic behavior can act as an internal water supplier during curing/hydration, increasing early-age strength</cite>. While this improves durability and may reduce cracking, it shifts carbon burdens to earlier, higher-temperature processing and more binder.

Quantitative comparison to conventional concrete

Multiple LCAs quantify hempcrete’s carbon intensity and show that, while buffering and plant sequestration can make hempcrete negative in some scenarios, its embodied carbon is often higher than conventional concrete assemblies due to lime and dosage, yet much lower operationally. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Industrial hemp absorbs 0.445 tons CO2 per ton of dry stems; this is stored in lime–hemp concrete and hemp composites, yielding a negative footprint</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Hemp-based boards achieved −2.302 kg CO2e/m2 versus +10.59 kg CO2e/m2 for gypsum; lime–hemp concrete walls ranged from +10.165 kg CO2e/m2 (pessimistic) to −9.696 kg CO2e/m2 (optimal), where sequestration and binder carbonation dominate</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Hempcrete masonry blocks can achieve −20.3168 kg CO2e due to uptake during growth and carbonation; untreated hempcrete sequesters −15.27 to −8.92 kg CO2e/m2, whereas traditional cavity walls emit 122.71 kg CO2e/m2</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-0">A building-scale LCEA/LCCA showed total energy over 50 years at ~50–10% of a conventional building and total carbon at ~50–10% of a conventional building, driven by hemp’s thermal–moisture moderation</cite>.

Mechanistically, hempcrete’s hygroscopic buffering increases embodied carbon via:
- Higher binder (lime) dosages to achieve workability and set with porous hemp hurds, as noted above. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-2">Hempcrete plasters need more binder than sand–lime coatings, increasing footprint</cite>.
- Transport and processing energy for hemp hurds and lime, and the need for lime kiln heat or unfired binder alternatives to reduce carbon. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-0">Hemp shives are waste but lime is energy‑intensive; replacing lime lowered total building carbon</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-2">Carbonation reabsorption is less than in mineral mortars; LCAs often omit this nuance</cite>.
- Additional protective layers or treatments to preserve hygroscopic cores in wet or freeze–thaw regimes, which add mass and emissions. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Sol–gel coatings raised hempcrete’s footprint to 22.51–28.77 kg CO2e/m2</cite>.

These numbers make clear that, even when hempcrete’s embodied carbon is positive in some scenarios, it is generally far lower in operational energy than conventional cavity walls, and can become net carbon negative over time when sequestration and carbonation are included. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Hemp-lime walls vary from +10 to −10 kg CO2e/m2 depending on conditions, while traditional cavity walls are ~123 kg CO2e/m2</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Hempcrete blocks can be strongly negative (−20 kg CO2e) due to plant uptake and carbonation</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-0">At the building scale, total carbon over 50 years can be ~10–50% of a conventional building because of reduced heating/cooling</cite>.

Why buffering can still be carbon “cheaper” at the system level

Even though hempcrete’s hygroscopic buffering raises embodied carbon relative to dense, impermeable concrete, the same buffering reduces building operational energy for thermal–humidity control, which can make the total cradle‑to‑gate life‑cycle lower for hempcrete assemblies. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-0">Hemp lime mixtures have low embodied energy and carbon, and they allow low operational energy by moderating indoor temperature and RH with minimal auxiliary heating/cooling</cite>. <cite id="ad8be665-1">Hemp-based concrete offers low environmental impact and high hygroscopic behavior; CO2 sequestered over the lifespan can exceed emissions during production, transport, and construction</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Rivas-Aybar et al. found −2.302 kg CO2e/m2 for hemp boards versus +10.59 for gypsum; hemp-lime concrete walls’ net emissions ranged from +10.165 to −9.696 kg CO2e/m2</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Hempcrete’s total over a 50-year building life can be 50–10% of a conventional building’s energy and carbon when accounting for reduced operation</cite>.

In other words, the hygroscopic buffering that increases material inputs (hemp hurds, lime, potential coatings) can be offset by large operational savings and, in many cases, net carbon sequestration, especially in climates with moderate RH and sufficient thermal buffering. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Industrial hemp sequesters substantial CO2 during growth, which is stored in hempcrete products</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Carbonation of lime in hempcrete contributes to sequestration, though to a lesser extent than in mineral mortars</cite>. <cite id="ad8be665-4">Design levers—binder type (low-impact lime or unfired binders), dosage, transport, construction method, and application technique—strongly influence the footprint</cite>.

Design levers to manage embodied carbon while preserving buffering

- Use low-impact binders and optimize dosage: <cite id="bb7d7c6b-0">Replacing lime with unfired binders cut total building carbon to ~50–10% of conventional over 50 years while preserving traditional properties</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-2">Optimizing consistency without excessive binder reduces footprint</cite>.
- Engineer for faster carbonation: <cite id="bb7d7c6b-2">Calcitic lime can capture ~90% CO2 per kg; accounting for carbonation in LCAs is often overlooked but improves net outcomes</cite>.
- Control moisture/thermal conditions to reduce protective layers: <cite id="ad8be665-2">Lime’s alkaline surface protects hemp from mold under climate swings</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Coatings can increase footprint; minimizing or targeting only high-RH zones preserves buffering while curbing embodied carbon</cite>.
- Favor assemblies where hempcrete acts as structural/insulating layer with timber framing: <cite id="ad8be665-4">Lime accounts for a large share of air pollution and energy in non-load-bearing hempcrete, motivating low-impact binders and timber support</cite>.
- Use plant-based systems where possible: <cite id="bb7d7c6b-0">Hemp shives are waste; leveraging biomass cycles lowers embodied energy and carbon relative to mineral-only systems</cite>.

Uncertainties and context dependence

Hygroscopic buffering’s carbon implications depend on climate, building physics, and assumptions. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Lime-hemp walls can swing from positive to negative footprint depending on sequestration vs emissions; traditional cavity walls consistently show much higher per‑area emissions</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-2">LCAs may undercount lime carbonation or overcount transport and dosage; sensitivity to binder choice and application technique is high</cite>. <cite id="ad8be665-2">Hempcrete’s breathability and moisture storage reduce mold risk and improve indoor air quality, but durability in aggressive environments may require protection that adds mass/CO2</cite>. Because buffering increases embodied carbon via sorbent materials and binder but reduces operational energy and can sequester CO2, the net life‑cycle benefit is strongest where thermal–moisture moderation is large and energy prices/emissions factors are high; in hot-dry or cold-dry climates with strong heating loads, the embodied penalty can be offset more readily than in arid climates with low diurnal RH swings.

Takeaway

Hempcrete’s hygroscopic moisture buffering increases embodied carbon relative to conventional concrete primarily by requiring sorbent hemp hurds and higher lime dosages to achieve hygrothermal control, with additional impacts from lime’s energy intensity and potential protective treatments. <cite id="ad8be665-0">Hemp’s hygroscopicity enables moisture buffering and internal curing, which can raise early strength but increase material/process energy</cite>. <cite id="2472abbd-0">Hemp concrete’s MBV (~2 g/(m2·%RH)) far exceeds conventional concrete’s (~0.37), evidencing stronger buffering but also greater absorbent mass</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-2">To achieve workable consistency, hempcrete often needs more binder than sand–lime coatings, elevating footprint</cite>. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-1">Nevertheless, hempcrete’s buffering yields large operational energy reductions and can be net carbon negative in favorable conditions, whereas conventional cavity walls emit ~123 kg CO2e/m2</cite>. The net life‑cycle outcome depends on material choices, dosage, climate, and system boundaries, with optimized hempcrete assemblies often achieving 50–10% of the carbon of conventional buildings over 50 years when operational savings are included. <cite id="bb7d7c6b-0">Building-scale LCAs show total carbon at ~50–10% of conventional buildings using hemp-lime composites</cite>.
</answer>

Snippet: Sustainability is of prime importance in the construction industry since building materials are a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions [1,2]. Concrete, in particular, is responsible for significant greenhouse gas emissions as a result of using cement as a binding agent. The use of plant-based materials has also been reported to be an effective substitute for chemicals in concrete construction. For example, the application of abaca fibre [4], kenaf cellulose microfiber [4] and eucalyptus fibre [5,6] to improve cracking and shrinkage properties; use of rice husk ash as supplementary cementitious materials to achieve ultra-high performance [7] and use of green artificial aggregate for curing [8].

Hempcrete, through the carbon sequestration process, stores carbon in it in a stable form and thus brings the net Green House Gas (GHG) emission to negative values during its manufacture and installation in building products [13]. Hemp tree stem has a highly porous anatomical structure allowing the absorption of large amounts of water with little change to the volume [14]. They are also considered hygroscopic, and, as such, hempbased concrete products (hempcrete) are often used in buildings to control moisture [15][16][17]. Herein, we propose that the hygroscopic behaviour of hemp could also be used to act as an internal supplier of water within a concrete mass during curing/hydration, and thus could increase the early age strength of concrete.

Snippet: The moisture buffering capacity is a hygroscopic parameter by means of which moisture-bearing materials in contact with the ambient air adsorb and desorb humidity to achieve an equal balance with the relative humidity of the ambient space [147]. There are a number of methods for measuring the buffering capacity of moisture, such as the Japanese standards [148], the Nordtest protocol [141], the method proposed by Padfield [149], the ISO standard [150], and the concept of the ultimate buffering value of moisture [151]. The cumulative amount of humidity buffered by the moisture-absorbing surface material at any time can be obtained from the quantity of water created less the water removed by all the moisture removal mechanisms [152] (Figure 16). 

Hemp concrete exhibits an impressive moisture buffer value (MBV) of 2 g/(m 2 •%RH), significantly exceeding the traditional concrete's MBV of 0.37 ± 0.04 g/(m 2 •%RH) [147,153]. The MBV measures a material's ability to absorb or release moisture in response to changes in relative humidity levels [107]. A higher MBV indicates a greater capacity for regulating ambient humidity. Unlike traditional concrete, hemp concrete maintains stable relative humidity and temperature conditions, unaffected by its moisture absorption or desorption behavior. MBV values vary based on application methods and thickness. For example, Lelievre et al. [154] recorded a value of 2.3 g/(m 2 •%RH), while sprayed and cast hemp concrete yielded approximately 2.14-2.15 g/(m 2 •%RH), respectively [155,156]. Title: Lime Hempcrete Composites Based on Unfired Binders. A Review
Snippet: Hempcrete has emerged as a viable and environmentally sound building material based on hemp lime mixture, whose properties render it a low Embodied Energy and Carbon (EE and EC) building material. Additionally, it allows a hempcrete building to achieve low Operational Energy and Carbon (OE and OC) by moderating indoor temperature and relative humidity fluctuations through the year with minimal auxiliary heating or cooling. Hemp shives used in hempcrete are a waste product, yet lime is an energy intensive material. This paper summarizes a research project the purpose of which was to investigate the possibility of substituting the lime in hempcrete with unfired binders, in part of whole, thus lowering the EE and EC of the mixture even further. Results of this research have shown that this is possible without compromising any of the traditional hempcrete properties, e.g., compressive strength and insulating value.
